title: Python on the web
game_role: The hero's profile card is drawn with your HTML.
objective: Understand how the web works with requests and responses, build HTML pages with Python and do routing
story: We're at the foot of Python Mountain! At the top stands a giant observation tower that receives messages from all over the world. Every message is a request, and every answer the tower gives is a response. Websites on the internet work exactly like this. Today we build our own web pages with Python.

sections.title: Request and response
sections.body:
What happens when you type an address into your browser:

- The browser sends a **request** to the server: "Give me the `/profile` page."
- The server reads the request, prepares the page and sends back a **response**.
- The response contains HTML and a **status code**.

The best-known status codes: `200` all good, `404` page not found, `500` something went wrong on the server.

sections.title: A site with Flask
sections.body:
One of the most loved ways to build websites in Python is the **Flask** package. On your own computer it looks like this: ```python from flask import Flask app = Flask(__name__) @app.route("/") def home(): return "

Welcome to Piko's site!

" app.run() ``` `@app.route("/")` says: "If someone asks for the `/` address, run the `home` function." In the examples we'll try the same idea with plain Python, without starting a server. To try Flask yourself: `pip install flask`.

sections.title: Building HTML with Python
sections.body:
A web server's main job is to turn data into HTML text. f-strings and `join` are enough for that: ```python name = "Piko" page = f"

Hello {name}

" items = ["sword", "potion"] html = "
    " + "".join(f"
  • {i}
    • " for i in items) + "
" ```

sections.title: Routing

examples.title: Build a page
examples.code:
name = "Piko" items = ["sword", "potion", "map"] page = f"

{name}'s bag

" page += "
    " + "".join(f"
  • {i}
    • " for i in items) + "
" print(page)

tasks.title: Welcome page
tasks.prompt:
`page` should be an HTML heading like `

Hello Piko

`. The name must come from the `name` variable.

tasks.title: List page
tasks.prompt:
Build an HTML list from `items`: `
  • sword
  • potion
` (no spaces or line breaks).
tasks.solution:
items = ["sword", "potion"] html = "
    " + "".join(f"
  • {i}
    • " for i in items) + "
" print(html)
hints: Join them all with "".join(...) and wrap them in <ul>.

tasks.title: Status code
tasks.prompt: The `status_text(code)` function should return `OK` for 200, `Not Found` for 404, `Server Error` for 500 and `Unknown` for anything else.
hints: You can use a dictionary and get().

challenge.title: Mini server
challenge.prompt:
The `handle(path)` function should return a `(status_code, html)` tuple. If the address is in `routes`, return `(200, page)`; otherwise `(404, "

Not Found

")`.
hints: Check with if path in routes:
Don't forget to call the function: routes[path]()

project_task.title: The game's web page
project_task.prompt:
Let's build the player profile page for Piko's Adventure. `render_profile(hero)` should return an HTML text containing: - `

Piko

` (the hero's name) - `

Health: 80

` - `

Gold: 35

`
project_task.solution:
def render_profile(hero): html = f"

{hero['name']}

" html += f"

Health: {hero['hp']}

" html += f"

Gold: {hero['gold']}

" return html print(render_profile({"name": "Piko", "hp": 80, "gold": 35}))
hints: Use different quotes when reading from a dictionary inside an f-string: {hero['name']}
Join the three parts with += and return it.
